extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, policymakers, applicants, and researchers (users of WIPO/IP systems)
extracted.subtask_description: Reference standards and eligibility requirements for various forms of intellectual property (patents, trademarks, industrial designs, geographical indications, plant variety protection) and the main international registration systems (Madrid, Hague, Lisbon, PCT, Budapest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for patent protection, the invention must be novel, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable, as judged by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core test applied by patent offices when assessing patent applications (novelty, non-obviousness/inventive step, industrial applicability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and disclosure obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years), during which patent holders can exploit their inventions exclusively; in return, applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public in a manner that enables others skilled in the art to replicate the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide sufficient written description enabling reproduction; term and disclosure are tradeoffs for exclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budapest Treaty — microorganism deposit for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention involves a microorganism and disclosure is not always possible in writing, deposit of a microorganism with any International Depositary Authority (IDA) under the Budapest Treaty is sufficient for patent procedure at national/regional offices that recognize the Treaty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit with an IDA eliminates need to deposit a microorganism in every country where protection is sought; IDAs provide receipt, storage and furnishing of samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance/renewal of IP rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance is the act of keeping an IP grant/registration in force primarily by paying required fees to the IP office. A trademark can be maintained indefinitely by paying renewal fees; patents, utility models and industrial designs can be maintained only for a limited number of years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay maintenance/renewal fees may cause lapse of protection; renewal intervals and maximum terms vary by IP right and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) procedure and national phase
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT System facilitates multiple national patent filings by providing an international phase (international search and possibly preliminary examination) followed by a national phase in which national/regional patent offices decide on patentability according to national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT simplifies procedural steps but grant decisions remain the prerogative of national/regional offices; applicants must enter national phase(s) to obtain enforceable patents in those jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority under Paris Convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The Paris Convention establishes a 'right of priority' enabling an IP applicant to claim priority of an earlier application filed up to 12 months previously for patents and utility models, and up to six months previously for trademarks and industrial designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority date is the filing date of the earlier application and is critical for determining novelty and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art definition
rubrics_metrics.description: All information disclosed to the public about an invention, in any form, before a given date; information on prior art assists in determining whether the claimed invention is new and involves an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art analysis is central to novelty and inventive-step determinations by patent examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family (WIPO definition) for statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO defines patent families as patent applications interlinked by one or more of: priority claim, PCT national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division. WIPO’s definition includes only families associated with patent applications for inventions and excludes those associated with utility model applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for harmonized statistical reporting of filings across jurisdictions; indicates filings related to the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark registration characteristics and territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely provided that the trademark holder pays the required renewal fees. Trademark rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the authority that has registered the trademark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing nationally or via international systems confers rights only in jurisdictions where registration is obtained; renewal obligations must be met to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System — international trademark filing and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System allows trademark holders to submit a single international application in one language (English, French or Spanish), pay a single set of fees (Swiss francs) and indicate the Madrid members where protection is sought (designations). The decision to issue a registration remains the prerogative of each designated national/regional IP office; rights remain limited to the jurisdiction of the office issuing registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madrid System simplifies filing and subsequent management (central recording of changes and renewals), but national refusals are possible and national law controls registrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification marks vs collective marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Certification marks are usually awarded for compliance with defined standards and may be used by anyone able to certify that products meet those standards. Collective marks distinguish characteristics (e.g., geographical origin, material, manufacture) of goods/services of different enterprises using the mark and are typically used only by members of an association or group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference affects who may use the mark and how rights are enforced; certification marks are not confined to membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes and class count (Nice/Locarno classifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes indicate categories of goods and services: the Nice Classification has 45 classes (34 goods, 11 services). The Locarno Classification (32 classes) is used for industrial designs. Class count is the number of classes specified in an application and affects filing/registration statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices use multi-class filing systems; others require separate single-class applications—affects costs and statistical comparisons across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design subject-matter and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial designs refer to the ornamental or aesthetic aspects of a useful article, including compositions of lines or colors or three-dimensional forms that give a special appearance to a product or handicraft. An industrial design can be protected if it is new or original; rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection prevents unauthorized copying/imitation; in some countries similar protection may be provided through design patents rather than design registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design term and renewals (Hague System notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a design is registered, the term of protection is generally five years and may be renewed for additional five-year periods up to a total of 15 years in most cases. The Hague System allows filing up to 100 different designs per application and centralizes management (recording changes/renewals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term lengths vary by jurisdiction (e.g., China: 10 years from application date). Hague System streamlines multi-territory filings but national refusals may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design count (in applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design count is the number of designs contained in an industrial design application or registration. Under the Hague System it is possible to obtain protection for up to 100 industrial designs in a single application (subject to class constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design count influences statistical comparison of application and registration numbers across offices; national offices differ in whether multi-design filings are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant breeder's rights eligibility (UPOV criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A breeder’s right is granted only when a variety is new, distinct, uniform and stable, and has a suitable denomination (title of protection granted when these conditions are met under UPOV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must file individual applications with each authority granting breeders’ rights; UPOV provides harmonized criteria for plant variety protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant Patent Act (PPA) scope in the USA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PPA, whoever invents or discovers and asexually reproduces any distinct and new variety of plant — including cultivated sports, mutants, hybrids and newly-found seedlings — other than a tuber-propagated plant or a plant found in an uncultivated state, may obtain a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPA covers asexually reproduced varieties; excludes tuber-propagated and wild-found plants as specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) scope in the USA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PVPA, the United States protects all sexually-reproduced plant varieties and tuber-propagated plant varieties, excluding fungi and bacteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PVPA and PPA are complementary frameworks covering different reproduction methods and types of plant material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication (GI) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographical indication is a sign identifying a good as originating in a specific geographical area and possessing a given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to that geographical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main function of a GI is to indicate connection between product quality/characteristics/reputation and territory of origin; GIs commonly used for agricultural/food products but also for handicrafts and manufactured goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI use requirements and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications can only be used on goods that conform to applicable requirements concerning the area of origin, processing method and typicity of the product. Goods from production sites outside the area of origin or goods that do not meet applicable requirements are prohibited from using the protected indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with origin and production specifications is essential to legitimately use a protected GI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellation of origin (stronger GI link)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellation of origin generally consists of a geographical name or traditional denomination designating a product as originating in a defined area where the quality or characteristics of the product are due exclusively or essentially to that geographical environment, including natural and human factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellations of origin are a more restrictive sub-category of GIs requiring a stronger link with the geographical area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection mechanisms for GIs (national and international)
rubrics_metrics.description: GIs are protected through a variety of legal means at national/regional levels, including sui generis systems (often registration-based), trademark law (collective and certification marks), unfair competition regulations, consumer protection laws, administrative and judicial decisions, and specific laws or decrees recognizing individual GIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different systems may coexist; protection obtained in one jurisdiction is territorially limited and international agreements or bilateral/regional lists may facilitate protection abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lisbon System — international protection for appellations/GIs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lisbon System facilitates international protection of appellations of origin via a single registration; registration with WIPO's International Bureau ensures protection in all Lisbon contracting parties for as long as the appellation remains protected in its contracting party of origin, but each contracting party may refuse protection within one year based on national/regional grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Geneva Act (2015) extended the Lisbon System to the broader category of GIs and made the system more flexible and open to intergovernmental organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System can be used for certain GIs (via trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications can be protected in several countries as trademarks (commonly collective and certification marks) through the Madrid System; however, trademarks incorporating geographical terms are not necessarily GIs and it can be difficult to determine exact numbers of registered GIs within trademark registries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection via Madrid/Trademark routes may coexist with sui generis GI regimes; national offices determine registrability under trademark law.

rubrics_metrics.name: National (direct/Paris) route vs international routes
rubrics_metrics.description: The national route (Paris/direct route) involves filing individual IP applications directly with each national/regional IP office; alternative international routes (Madrid, Hague, PCT) provide centralized filing/management but decisions on protection remain with national/regional offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of route affects procedural burden, costs, and timing; international systems simplify filing and subsequent management but do not eliminate national substantive examinations or refusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and grant — territorial and temporal nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is the exclusive set of rights accorded to an applicant when an industrial design or trademark is registered; grants (patents) similarly accord exclusive rights when issued. As with other IP rights, the effects are limited to the territory of the jurisdiction issuing the right and, except for some trademarks, are time-limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain protection abroad, rights must be sought under relevant national/regional laws or via international agreements/systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application and equivalent grant (WIPO counting methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications/grants at regional offices are treated as equivalent to multiple national applications/grants—one in each member state—for statistical reporting. WIPO's equivalent application/grant calculations vary by regional office and are used to report data by origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statistical definition to unduplicate/report filings and grants across regional offices and member states consistently.
